Considering species, habitat pressures and existing policies strengthens conservation impact

","resourceUsed":"227 species occurrences","excerpt":"Considering species, habitat pressures and existing policies strengthens conservation impact... Cumulative impact assessment (CIA) frameworks are widely used to evaluate complex interactions between…","body":"

Cumulative impact assessment (CIA) frameworks are widely used to evaluate complex interactions between multiple anthropogenic stressors on ecosystems. CIAs have supported international policies such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals to balance both environmental protection and blue economy development in marine environments, but their application at finer scales is currently insufficient. This study integrated species distribution models (SDMs) with CIA frameworks to evaluate how policy choices impact estuarine ecosystems in China, focusing on the Shanghai Coastal Marine Spatial Planning (CMSP 2021–2035) and the Yangtze River Estuary 10-year fishing ban (2021–2031) policies.

Studied Yangtze River Estuary, the authors considered impacts to three local species - Chinese sturgeon (Acipenser sinensis), Chinese mitten crab (Eriocheir sinensis), and Osbeck's grenadier anchovy (Coilia mystus). They constructed a scenario-based CIA framework that combined SDMs, species-specific vulnerability to human pressures and different policy scenarios to assess how management approaches could affect cumulative pressures on the habitats of multiple species. The authros used biodiversity records from both GBIF and OBIS to construct MaxEnt SDMs.

The findings identified pollution, shipping, coastal infrastructure development and fishing as the dominant anthropogenic pressures affecting the species’ habitats. They found that the 10-year fishing ban policy had a large effect on reducing habitat pressure, but in combination with the CMSP policy, adding the fishing ban produced only a modest additional reduction. This suggests that the CMSP policy provides a more comprehensive management approach for habitat conservation as it addresses a broader range of pressures. The authors note that this assessment is based on habitat-level pressures not guidance for population-level fisheries management.

The integrated SDM and CIA framework highlights the importance of considering both species spatial patterns and policy scenarios for informing the management of complex anthropogenic pressures in estuaries.
